title: Is the lifelike mountain picture better than the column graph?
description: An imaginary mountain range holds all seven tallest mountains and looks more realistic than the column graph. Its look is tested against the heights in the table. Keeko doubts this and says the lifelike picture is better because it looks more real.
teaching_notes: One idea: a picture that looks real can still be wrong, so we test what it shows against the numbers of the table. Watch for students who trust a picture because it looks good.

source: Is the infographic better than the column graph?
video_script.why: The child tests what a lifelike mountain range seems to show against the heights of the table, and finds that it looks real but is not accurate.
video_script.substitution: The mountain range of the book is tested against the heights of the table.
video_script.anchor: an imaginary mountain range holding the seven tallest mountains, beside the column graph with columns of equal width
video_script.wrong_answer: the lifelike picture is better because it looks more real
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko trusts the lifelike picture because it looks more real. Doubling Elbrus gives more than the height of Everest, though the picture shows Everest as twice as tall, so the picture is not accurate and the claim is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The picture looks more realistic, but it is not accurate

final_answer.value: Looks more realistic but is not accurate: for example Everest appears twice as tall as Elbrus although it is not.
final_answer.spoken: it looks more realistic, but it is not accurate

maths_rules: Everest is 8848 m and Elbrus is 5642 m
in the picture, Everest appears to be twice as tall as Elbrus
5642 is more than 5000, so twice Elbrus is more than 2 x 5000 = 10000
8848 is less than 10000, so Everest is shorter than twice Elbrus
so the picture shows a height ratio that the numbers do not give; it is not accurate
video_script.design: The lifelike mountain range is set beside the column graph. One claim of the picture, that Everest is twice Elbrus, is tested by rounding Elbrus down to 5000 and doubling.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the tallest mountains.
<bookmark mark='range'/>An imaginary mountain range holds all seven mountains. The peaks look very real.
<bookmark mark='cols'/>The column graph has plain columns of equal width.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The mountains look more realistic, but is the picture accurate?

beats.on_screen: the two pictures stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the range with one claim lit: Everest looks twice as tall as Elbrus

marks.claim: the peaks of Everest and Elbrus are lit, and Everest looks twice as tall as Elbrus

narration: <bookmark mark='claim'/>To test a picture, we pick one thing it shows. Here, Everest looks twice as tall as Elbrus.

beats.on_screen: Given: Mount Everest 8848 m; Mount Elbrus 5642 m; in the picture Everest looks twice as tall as Elbrus

marks.given: the two heights and the claim are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, Everest is eight thousand eight hundred and forty eight metres. Elbrus is five thousand six hundred and forty two metres.

beats.on_screen: To find: do the numbers agree with the picture, and is the picture accurate?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find if the numbers agree with the picture.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: twice Elbrus, using 5000 m, which is less than 5642 m: 2 x 5000 = 10000 m

marks.round: the height of Elbrus is rounded down to five thousand
marks.double: the doubling two times five thousand is written

narration: <bookmark mark='round'/>Step one, take Elbrus as five thousand metres, which is less than its real height.
<bookmark mark='double'/>Twice five thousand is ten thousand. Twice the real height of Elbrus is even more than that.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: Everest is 8848 m, which is less than 10000 m

marks.cmp: the height of Everest is placed beside the ten thousand metre mark
marks.low: the bar of Everest falls short of the mark

narration: <bookmark mark='cmp'/>Step two, compare with Everest, which is eight thousand eight hundred and forty eight metres.
<bookmark mark='low'/>That is less than ten thousand, so Everest is shorter than twice Elbrus.

beats.on_screen: Answer: The picture looks more realistic, but it is not accurate: Everest appears twice as tall as Elbrus although it is not

marks.ans: the answer is boxed beside the mountain range

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The picture looks more realistic, but it is not accurate. Everest appears twice as tall as Elbrus, although it is not.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says the lifelike picture is better because it looks more real; the doubled Elbrus peak rises above Everest; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.over: a peak of twice the height of Elbrus rises above the peak of Everest

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the lifelike picture is better because it looks more real.
<bookmark mark='over'/>But twice Elbrus rises above Everest, which the picture does not show.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>A good picture must agree with the numbers, and that matters more than looking real.
